quotes.text: Throwing rollicking piano and organ solos and entertaining-as-hell guitar work into a stew with Jim Morrison's dark, mystical lyrics and good singing voice, and not showing reluctance to draw upon other sources when needed, the Doors created a sound that you may love or you may hate, but you cannot deny was fiercely original and unique.
their debut created a style and atmosphere totally uncharacteristic of the times, filled with darkness, despair, and ... stupid pop songs a la "I Looked At You."

their second album took the style of the first, weeded out everything bad from the debut, expanded upon and added to that which worked, and in the process created one of the finest albums of all time.

the group started incorporating some blues rock elements. And say what you will, but given the fact that the band was never a real 'blues band', this made their sound on the next two albums reaaaaally interesting.
The intelligence shown in his arrangments astounds me, and as much as anybody he made his parts exciting.

As a guitarist, Robbie was just what the band needed. Nothing too flashy, and feedback was never a serious part of his bag-o-tricks, but as far as 'just playing the guitar' went, he was fabulous. Good solos, good riff-work, knowledge of when to mess around in the studio, etc.
Musically, the album incorporates a wide range of styles, including jazz, blues, classical, pop, and R&B, all anchored in a rock foundation.
The Doors developed much of the material for their debut during live performances in 1966, particularly at the Whisky a Go Go in Los Angeles.
Rothchild had forbidden Krieger from using any of his guitar effects (particularly the wah wah pedal) on the record in order to avoid what Rothchild thought was the overuse of these devices.
According to Botnick, "What you hear on the first album is what they did live. It wasn't just playing the song–it transcended that."
Session musician Larry Knechtel and Krieger overdubbed bass guitar on several tracks in order to give some "punch" to the sound of Manzarek's keyboard bass.
Morrison explained in 1969, "We started almost immediately, and some of the songs took only a few takes. We'd do several takes just to make sure we couldn't do a better one."
Ray Manzarek's organ was pretty foundational to The Doors' sound, but became increasingly anachronistic as the 70s starting figuring out what it wanted to be.

The first thing that strikes me about Morrison Hotel is that the band seems to just be having a lot of fun. There are no orchestral pretensions à la The Soft Parade, no "The End" / "When the Music's Over" level epics – it just sounds like The Doors cutting loose and having a great time.
"Roadhouse Blues" sets that tone right from the get-go – it sounds like they really are a band in some rundown roadhouse somewhere just playing for the hell of it.
There are far more technically skilled singers who have no idea how to put excitement into a song like Jim Morrison could.
"Roadhouse Blues" may be the best song The Doors ever did when they weren't feeling ambitious, and just wanted to kick out their particular brand of blues.

I'm blown away by how they took the 50s template from Ritchie Valens' "Ooh, My Head" and any one of a number of Eddie Cochran songs and updated it with a harder edge. I mean, it is pretty much a perfect approximation of what it would sound like to take a 50s song and transplant it to 1970, the band did a remarkable job of translating what is a 50s song in form and structure into the language of the times.
even if you don't care for their music, you have to admit that no one sounds like The Doors. Even when they're doing old blues numbers they have a singular sound and an undeniable presence.
With a superb sense of erotic dynamics, they turn down the heat to deliver a few more teasing caresses, then thrust-thrust (breathe) thrust-thrust and they're slamming it home again.

John Densmore is fabulous with the shifts from Brazilian to thrash and Robby Krieger executes a Paul Butterfield-influenced riff with surprising precision. Ray Manzarek is one of the few organists I actually enjoy, for he played with a clipped, rhythmic style that's so much cleaner than the big organ sound you hear in people like Lee Michaels.

His melodic range may have been limited, but his dynamic range is unparalleled, as we will see throughout this album. Mastery of dynamics is a tricky thing; often when singers attempt to lower the volume and ramp it back up it can sound contrived. Jim Morrison had the skills of a trained stage actor when it came to dynamics; each line he delivers is often a product of discipline and patience.
It's also fairly obvious that his singing style influenced Kurt Cobain's.
The Doors' lyrics are often full of surprising words and phrases you don't expect to hear in popular music, and their expressionistic world-view led to some very memorable imagery.
